odds.lifeTitle: 💫 How does life really change before and after winning?
odds.lifeDesc: Not rumors, things confirmed by actual research
odds.life1Tag: Most winners go broke within a few years?
odds.life1: This is an unfounded myth. The National Endowment for Financial Education, which supposedly published the 70% go broke stat, officially denied ever conducting such a study. A 15-year Swedish tracking study found winners actually kept their wealth better than non-winners.
odds.life2: Contrary to rumors, the change is nowhere near that dramatic — divorce rates only rise modestly. What is more interesting: friendships get shaken up more than marriages, since money often triggers a reshuffling of who your real friends are.
odds.life3Tag: Winners quit their job right away?
odds.life3: It depends on the amount, winners of over 10 million dollars mostly do leave the workforce, but below that, about half keep working. It seems the connection to other people and sense of purpose matters more than the money itself.
odds.life4Tag: So, does it make you happier?
odds.life4: Day-to-day mood does not jump dramatically, but the feeling of being satisfied with my life stays noticeably higher for over 10 years. The real challenge is not managing the money, it is managing family and friends expectations.

faq.q1: How much tax is actually deducted? 😮
faq.a1:
👉 US residents get 24% withheld upfront, settled up to 37% later when filing.

👉 Non-US residents (including Korean residents) have 30% withheld by the US first — once home-country tax is added on top, larger jackpots often lose over 40% of the total to tax. Check the calculator above for your exact number.
faq.q2: Wait, I pay tax in Korea too?
faq.a2: Yes. US lottery winnings aren’t a domestic lottery, so they’re combined into comprehensive income tax (up to 45%). Tax already paid in the US can offset via Foreign Tax Credit (FTC).
faq.q3: Can I get back the tax I paid in the US? 💸
faq.a3: The 30% US federal withholding is practically non-refundable. State tax varies — Maryland and Arizona are unusual in taxing non-residents too. Pick your winning state below to check.

faq.q4: Will my health insurance premium spike if I win? 🏥
faq.a4:
Regional subscribers see winnings fully counted as income, raising premiums a lot.

Employed subscribers pay extra premium above ₩20M/year in outside income too.

If registered as a dependent, you may lose that status.
faq.q5: I’m already receiving National Pension / Basic Pension — does this affect it? 👴
faq.a5:
Depends on the program. National Pension — if already receiving it, the reduction rule applies to earned/business income, not a one-time windfall.

Basic Pension / welfare benefits reassess eligibility by income and assets, so benefits could change.

(Basic Pension is generally for Korean nationals only — foreign residents in Korea only need to check the National Pension reduction rule.)
faq.q6: How do I tell if a "you won" message is a scam? 🚨
faq.a6:
Common scam patterns: impersonating card companies asking for card info to "refund" a losing ticket,

fake lottery commission asking for crypto purchases,

or selling fake winning-number predictions.

Real winnings are checked by you on the official site — unsolicited requests for money or info are 100% scams.
faq.q7: How much gift tax if I share with family? 👨‍👩‍👧
faq.a7: Spouse up to ₩600M, adult children up to ₩50M are tax-free. Amounts above that face a 10–50% progressive rate. Filing on time gets you a 3% credit.
faq.q7us: How much gift tax if I share with family? 👨‍👩‍👧
faq.a7us: As of 2026, you can give up to $19,000 per person per year with no filing required at all. Give more than that, and you’ll need to file a gift tax return — but you still won’t actually owe any tax until your lifetime gifts pass the $15 million exemption. For almost everyone, that means you can share freely without worrying about gift tax.
faq.q7cn: How much gift tax if I share with family? 👨‍👩‍👧
faq.a7cn: China has no dedicated gift tax on cash gifts between individuals — you don’t need to worry about tax when giving cash to a spouse, parent, or child. Gifting real estate is a separate matter with its own taxes (like deed tax), so check that separately if it applies.
faq.q7in: How much gift tax if I share with family? 👨‍👩‍👧
faq.a7in: Gifts to specified relatives (spouse, parents, siblings, children, etc.) are tax-free regardless of amount. However, cash gifts or receipts exceeding ₹200,000 (about 2 lakh) can trigger a separate penalty under Section 269ST of the Income Tax Act, so it's safer to split large amounts via bank transfer.
faq.q8: Is prize money subject to property division in a divorce? 💍
faq.a8: In principle, no — courts treat it as personal property from pure luck. But if a spouse helped preserve or grow the money afterward, that contribution may be included.
faq.q9: By when do I have to claim the winnings? ⏰
faq.a9: Usually 90 days to 1 year. Miss it, and it reverts to the state — gone forever. One winner actually lost $138M by missing the deadline.
faq.q10: Aside from the lottery, might I have unclaimed money that’s already mine?
faq.a10: Unlike the lottery, this money is already confirmed as yours — the story’s different here. According to Korea’s National Tax Service, unclaimed national tax refunds add up to hundreds of billions of won every year. If you don’t claim it within 5 years of the first possible claim date, it reverts to the state treasury and you lose it for good. Check the list below to see if any of these apply to you.
faq.checklistTitle: Check if any of these apply to you
faq.check1: Changed jobs or left a job in the last 5 years
faq.check2: Worked as a freelancer/contractor and might have skipped filing some year
faq.check3: Left a job mid-year and never checked if you overpaid that year’s taxes
faq.check4: Might have missed deductions (medical, donations, etc.) in some year
faq.check5: Paid local taxes (car tax, property tax, etc.) but never rechecked
faq.check6: Have an old bank account, uncashed check, or insurance payout you forgot about
faq.check7: Your health insurance / national pension eligibility changed (job change, resignation, etc.) but you never checked
faq.check8: Haven’t used your card points in years and just left them
faq.checkDefault: If any apply, check for real below 👇
faq.checklistFooter: We can’t do the lookup for you directly — these are government systems that require resident registration number verification — but we’ve linked you straight to the real official channels. Takes about 10 minutes to check.
faq.q11: Is it better to take it all at once, or in installments?
faq.a11: US lottery jackpots can be paid two ways — ① annuity (spread over 29 years) or ② lump sum (paid at once, but only about 45–60% of the announced amount). The jackpot in the news is based on ①. Most winners choose ② — check the for a detailed comparison.
faq.q12: Where can I buy a US lottery ticket?
faq.a12: It's safest to buy directly at convenience stores or gas stations in the US. If you use an online purchase-agent service instead, its legality varies by country, so check whether it's legal where you live before using one.
faq.q13: What if a friend buys a ticket for me, or claims the prize on my behalf?
faq.a13:
Even a friend buying it personally creates complications. Ownership is usually determined by who signs to claim it.

If they claim as a US resident, their tax rate applies, and transferring the money could trigger US gift tax on their end, plus gift tax rules in whichever country you live in.
faq.q14: Where can I check past winning numbers?
faq.a14b: We show recent numbers on our home screen, but the official sites are the most accurate source.
faq.q15: Can I claim winnings without US citizenship?
faq.a15: Yes, foreigners who legally bought a ticket can claim. Non-resident aliens face the 30% withholding though.
faq.q16: I’m a Korean living in the US — which option should I choose? (students, expats, green card, citizens)
faq.a16: “Living in the US” and “US tax resident” can differ. Green card/citizenship holders should pick “US.” Students or early-stage expats may still be non-resident aliens, making “Korea (non-resident)” more accurate. Consult a US tax pro if unsure.
faq.ftcFlow1: 30% is automatically withheld when you receive your prize in the US
faq.ftcFlow2: After returning to Korea, file it as other income in your comprehensive income tax return the following May
faq.ftcFlow3: When filing, apply for FTC with the documents below to offset the tax you already paid in the US
faq.ftcChecklistTitle: Before applying for FTC, have you gathered these documents?
faq.ftcDoc1: Certificate of tax payment issued by the foreign government (US)
faq.ftcDocsDefault: Check the boxes to see how ready you are to file
faq.q17: What is the "filing status (single/married)" option in the calculator?
faq.a17: US filing status affects tax brackets, but for lottery-size amounts it barely matters — the difference between single and joint top brackets is a rounding error.
faq.q18: What actually happens, step by step, if I win?
faq.a18: It’s a 6-step process: buy in the US → confirm the win → claim it. See the full breakdown under A closer look at the purchase process below.
faq.q19: How do I file these taxes?
faq.a19: The US withholds 30% first; in Korea you report it as other income the following May. Tax paid in the US can offset via FTC. Consult a tax pro handling both countries.
faq.q19us: How do I file these taxes?
faq.a19us: As a US resident, you report the winnings as "Other Income" on your federal return (Form 1040, Schedule 1). For large amounts you’ll typically get a W-2G showing 24% withheld upfront — that’s just a down payment against your actual tax rate (up to 37%), so you may owe more or get some back when you file. Depending on the state, you may also need to file a separate state return.
faq.q19cn: How do I file these taxes?
faq.a19cn: The US withholds 30% first. In China, this income is classified as "incidental income" (偶然所得) taxed at a flat 20%, which you self-report between March 1 and June 30 of the following year via the "个人所得税" app or the natural person e-tax portal (per MOF/STA Announcement No. 3 of 2020). Tax already paid in the US can offset this through the foreign tax credit.
faq.q19in: How do I actually file the tax return?
faq.a19in: The US withholds 30% first. In India, you report this prize income under Schedule FSI (Foreign Source Income) of your income tax return (ITR). To claim a foreign tax credit for the US withholding, you must also file Form 67 (reorganized as Form 44 under the 2026 rules) by the ITR filing deadline, and the amount in it must exactly match Schedule FSI.
faq.q20: How do I claim the Foreign Tax Credit (FTC)? What documents do I need?
faq.a20:
To offset the US tax (30% withholding) against your Korean income tax filing, based on a July 2026 National Tax Service phone consultation you’ll need: a certificate of tax payment issued by the foreign (US) government, a payment receipt, a withholding tax receipt, and proof of the prize itself.

The exchange rate used is the rate on the day you actually received the prize money (per Enforcement Decree of the Income Tax Act, Article 50).

This isn’t an official written ruling, so confirm the exact document list with a tax professional before filing.
faq.q21: Do I owe Korean tax even if I haven't lived in Korea long? ⚠️
faq.a21:
This isn't a simple yes/no. Under a proviso in Article 3 of Korea's Income Tax Act, a resident who has lived in Korea 5 years or less within the most recent 10 years (based on length of residence, not nationality) has a special rule: foreign-source income is only taxed in Korea if it's actually remitted to or received within Korea.

However, whether this actually applies to migrant workers (e.g. E-9 visa holders) is unclear and may be interpreted differently case by case — if you already have your life based in Korea and are working continuously, tax authorities may view it differently.

Don't assume "no remittance means no tax" — if you really do win, talk to a tax professional right away to get an answer specific to your situation.

faq.qTaxTerms: What do withholding tax, progressive tax, FTC, and more even mean? 📖
faq.aTaxTerms:
👉 Withholding tax: the payer (the US) takes the tax out first and pays you the rest — it's not your final bill, just money taken upfront.

👉 Progressive tax: the tax rate rises as income rises — US federal tax tops out at 37%, Korean comprehensive income tax at 45%.

👉 Foreign Tax Credit (FTC): lets tax already paid in the US be subtracted again when your home country calculates your tax, so the same income isn't taxed twice.

👉 Tax treaty: an agreement between two countries promising not to tax the same income twice — if one exists, it can change how your tax is calculated.

👉 Tax credit: an amount subtracted directly from the tax you already owe, not from your income — different from a deduction, which lowers the income used to calculate tax.

👉 Offset: matching what's owed against what's already been paid and settling only the difference — crediting US tax against Korean tax is one example.

👉 Surcharge: an extra charge added on top of the tax itself, like a markup — it only applies to very large incomes, and only in some countries like India or Pakistan.

👉 Double taxation: when two countries each tax the same income, so you end up paying tax on it twice — credits like FTC exist to prevent or reduce this.

👉 Windfall gain: money you get unexpectedly rather than by working for it — like lottery winnings, gifts, or prizes — some countries tax it differently from wage income.

👉 Effective tax rate: your real tax rate after all deductions and surcharges — actual tax paid divided by total income — usually different from (and more accurate than) the rate written in the law.

👉 Tax base: the amount the tax rate actually gets applied to, right before multiplying — often your income minus deductions, so it can be smaller than what you actually received.

👉 Separate taxation: taxing one type of income on its own, at a fixed rate, without combining it with your other income — Korean lottery winnings are taxed this way, but US lottery winnings must be combined into your comprehensive income tax filing.

👉 Tax-exempt: no tax is charged at all — like gifts to a spouse up to 600 million won, which are tax-free up to that legal limit.
faq.qGameBasics: What exactly are Powerball and Mega Millions? 🎱
faq.aGameBasics: They're the US's two big multi-state lotteries. You pick numbers, and the more of them match the draw, the bigger your prize — match all of them and you win the jackpot. Powerball draws Mon/Wed/Sat, Mega Millions draws Tue/Fri. For price, number format, and odds side by side, see 📚 More details → Let's start with the basics below.
faq.qJackpotEst: Why does the home page jackpot keep changing? Is it the real, exact amount? 🔄
faq.aJackpotEst: If no one wins, the prize rolls over and keeps growing. The number shown is an estimate based on ticket sales, so it keeps shifting until a few days before the draw, when it's finalized. It's also based on the annuity (29-year payout) — taking it as a lump sum gets you only about 45–60% of that.
faq.q19vn: How do I actually file taxes if I live in Vietnam?
faq.a19vn: The US withholds 30% first. Vietnam classifies this as "prize income" (trúng thưởng) and applies a flat 10% rate to the portion over 10 million VND per occurrence (the exemption threshold rose to 20 million VND under the new income tax law effective July 1, 2026, but jackpot-sized winnings always exceed it either way). Vietnam has no ratified tax treaty with the US, but under domestic law (Circular 111/2013/TT-BTC, Article 26.2) you can still offset the US tax against your Vietnamese tax bill regardless of treaty status. Unlike salary income, which goes through an annual finalization each May, prize income is declared separately each time it's received — please confirm the exact filing form and process with a Vietnamese tax professional.

faq.q19id: How do I actually file taxes on this?
faq.a19id: The US withholds 30% first. In Indonesia, this income is classified as a lottery prize final tax (Income Tax Article 4(2), Pasal 4(2)) at a flat 25% rate. Since there's no Indonesian withholding agent for a US-issued lottery, you must self-report it within 3 months after the tax year ends (usually by March 31) on your Annual Individual Income Tax Return (SPT Tahunan, Form 1770), under the Final Tax section (SPT PPh Final). Since 2025, filing goes through the unified Coretax DJP system instead of the old pajak.go.id.
faq.q19ph: How do I actually file taxes on this?
faq.a19ph: The US withholds 30% first. In the Philippines, this winning doesn't qualify for the 20% final tax reserved for domestic PCSO lottery prizes, so it's taxed as ordinary income at progressive rates (up to 35%). Depending on your income type, you report it on your annual income tax return (BIR Form 1700 or 1701), usually due April 15 of the following year. To claim a foreign tax credit, you'll need to attach receipts or certificates proving the US tax paid — the credit is capped by the formula (Philippine tax × foreign income / worldwide income).
home.taxTermProgressiveDesc: The tax rate rises as income rises — US federal tax tops out at 37%, Korean comprehensive income tax at 45%.

odds.winner4: September 2011, Georgia — Kathy Scruggs went to buy a Mega Millions ticket, but the clerk mistakenly handed her a Powerball ticket instead. The winning ticket turned out to be that very ‘wrong’ one — unemployed after her seasonal job had ended, she walked away with $15.12 million in cash. She didn’t realize she’d won until the night after the drawing, and woke up her whole family to tell them.
compare.otherLangSub: Tapping one opens that country's tax guide, not the calculator.
faq.a19jp: The US withholds 30% first. Japan classifies this prize as "occasional income" (一時所得, National Tax Agency Tax Answer No.1490) — only half of (winnings minus a ¥500,000 special deduction) is added to your other income and taxed at progressive rates. File during the final tax return period (Feb 16–Mar 15 of the following year); tax already paid in the US can be offset via the foreign tax credit (外国税額控除).
faq.a19th: The US withholds 30% first. ⚠️ We couldn't find clear official guidance on exactly how Thai residents must report foreign lottery winnings — under Revenue Department Order Paw.161/2566 (effective 2023), the broad rule is that winnings remitted into Thailand get combined with that year's assessable income and reported on Form PND.90 by March 31 of the following year (early April for e-filing). Check the exact procedure and whether a foreign tax credit applies with a Thai tax advisor.
faq.a19ru: The US withholds 30% first. Russia applies the regular progressive personal income tax (5 brackets since the 2025 reform, up to 22%) to foreign lottery winnings, with no withholding — you self-report via Form 3-NDFL by April 30 of the following year (tax due by July 15). ⚠️ Russia suspended key articles of the US-Russia tax treaty (including double-tax relief) by Presidential Decree No.585 in 2023. Whether this also blocks the foreign tax credit is disputed among specialists — some say the domestic-law credit (Tax Code Art.232) still applies independently of the treaty, others say the suspension makes it moot in practice. Check with a Russian tax professional before filing.
faq.a19np: The US withholds 30% first. Nepal classifies this as a "windfall gain" (Income Tax Act Section 88A) taxed at a flat 25% with no deductions — self-assessed and filed with the Inland Revenue Department within 3 months of the fiscal year end (mid-July). Tax paid in the US can be credited against Nepal's tax under Section 71 (foreign tax credit), limited to Nepal's average rate.
faq.a19lk: The US withholds 30% first. Sri Lanka doesn't apply its lottery withholding rules (Sections 157-158, which only cover Sri Lanka-sourced payouts) to foreign winnings — instead the regular progressive personal income tax (up to 36% for 2025/26) applies, self-filed online with the Inland Revenue Department (e-filing mandatory; the 2025/26 deadline is Nov 30, 2026). ⚠️ It's unclear whether a 15% preferential rate introduced in 2025 for remitted foreign income also covers windfall gains like lottery winnings.
faq.a19uz: The US withholds 30% first. Uzbekistan taxes all personal income, including lottery winnings, at a flat 12% (since the 2023 reform). If you have foreign income, file a declaration with your local tax office (or via my3.soliq.uz) by April 1 of the following year, with tax due by June 1.
faq.a19kz: The US withholds 30% first. Under Kazakhstan's new Tax Code (Law No.214-VIII, effective 2026), Article 379 ("income in the form of winnings") applies a flat 10% rate for residents with no withholding. To claim a foreign tax credit for US tax paid, file an individual income tax return (Form 240.00/270.00) by September 15 of the following year.
faq.a19kg: The US withholds 30% first. Kyrgyzstan applies a flat 10% rate to personal income including winnings; since there is no local withholding agent for a foreign payout, you must self-report using the unified tax declaration (Form 102) with the State Tax Service by April 1 of the following year.
faq.a19mm: The US withholds 30% first. Myanmar classifies this as "Income from Other Sources" — separate from its own state lottery's preferential treatment — taxed at progressive rates (top bracket 25%, over 70 million kyats). File with the Internal Revenue Department within 3 months of the end of Myanmar's tax year (October–September).
faq.a19bd: The US withholds 30% first. Bangladesh classifies lottery/prize winnings as "Income from Other Sources," taxed at a flat 25% with no deductions. File via the NBR e-filing portal by November 30 following the end of the income year (July-June) — though this deadline is often extended.
faq.a19pk: The US withholds 30% first. ⚠️ Pakistan's Income Tax Ordinance Section 156 (20-40% withholding on lottery prizes) assumes a Pakistan-based payer, so it's unclear whether it applies to winnings paid directly from the US. Since Pakistan taxes residents on worldwide income, you must self-file via the FBR IRIS portal by September 30 of the following year; US tax paid can be credited under Section 103 (this calculator conservatively approximates using the general top rate of 35% plus an 8% super tax and 10% surcharge).
faq.a19kh: The US withholds 30% first. ⚠️ We couldn't find a clear provision in Cambodia's tax law covering individual lottery/prize income outside of salary or business income — Cambodia generally taxes on a territorial basis, so foreign-sourced income is often considered outside scope, but this isn't a settled interpretation. If you actually win, confirm your specific situation with the General Department of Taxation (GDT) or a local tax advisor.
faq.a19mn: The US withholds 30% first. ⚠️ Mongolia banned domestic betting/lottery/online gambling in May 2025, and the related tax provisions — including the old 40% rate on gambling winnings — appear to have been repealed along with it; we couldn't find a replacement provision specifically for foreign lottery winnings. It may fall under employment/other income (flat 10%) as the closest candidate, used here as a tentative estimate. Since there's no withholding agent, you'd self-file with your local tax office by February 15 of the following year.
faq.a19la: The US withholds 30% first. Under Laos's new Income Tax Law (No.88/NA, effective July 2026), lottery winnings are taxed at a flat 5% (amounts up to 10 million kip are exempt, though jackpot-scale winnings always exceed that). Laos has no tax treaty with the US, so no foreign tax credit applies — Laos's 5% simply stacks on top of the US withholding. Confirm the exact filing deadline with Lao tax authorities.
faq.a7jp: Japan gives each recipient an annual basic exemption of ¥1.1 million; amounts above that are taxed at progressive rates up to 55%. Couples married 20+ years can gift up to ¥20 million in a home tax-free (separate from the basic exemption), and parents/grandparents 60+ can gift up to ¥25 million tax-free to children/grandchildren 18+ under the "settlement at inheritance" system (later reconciled against inheritance tax).
faq.a7vn: In Vietnam, gifts between family — spouse, parents, children, grandparents, grandchildren, siblings — are fully tax-exempt (Circular 111/2013/TT-BTC, Article 23). Gifts from non-family are taxed at a flat 10% on the amount exceeding 10 million VND per gift (rising to 20 million VND from July 2026).
faq.a7id: Under Indonesia's Income Tax Law Article 4(3), gifts between direct first-degree relatives (parent to child) are fully exempt as long as there's no business, employment, or ownership relationship involved. Gifts outside that direct line — like between siblings or grandparent-grandchild — are taxed at the regular progressive rate (Article 17), and gifting real estate triggers a separate transfer tax (BPHTB).
faq.a7ph: In the Philippines, the donor gets an annual exemption of ₱250,000; anything above that is taxed at a flat 6% regardless of the relationship (TRAIN law). File and pay the donor's tax return (BIR Form 1800) within 30 days of the donation.
faq.a7th: In Thailand, gifts to descendants, ascendants, or a spouse are exempt up to 20 million baht/year, with a 5% rate above that. Gifts to others are exempt up to 10 million baht/year, also taxed at 5% above that.
faq.a7ru: In Russia, gifts of cash or property between close relatives — spouse, parents, children, grandparents, grandchildren, siblings — are fully tax-exempt. Gifts to non-relatives must be self-reported via Form 3-NDFL, taxed at 13% up to 2.4 million rubles and 15% above that.
faq.a7np: Under Nepal's Income Tax Act Section 10(f), gifts arising from family affection — a parent's allowance, wedding gift money, a relative's property gift — are fully exempt. This is a completely separate category from "windfall gains" like lottery winnings, which are taxed at 25%.
faq.a7lk: Sri Lanka currently has no separate gift tax on individuals — gifts themselves aren't taxed, regardless of family or non-family. You do need to disclose gifted assets received during the year on your annual statement of assets, though.
faq.a7uz: Uzbekistan has no separate inheritance or gift tax. That said, personal income tax may still apply depending on the type and source of the gifted property, so while sharing cash with family generally isn't a big tax concern, gifting larger assets like real estate is worth checking separately.
faq.a7kz: In Kazakhstan, the value of property received as a gift from another individual is excluded from taxable income — there's no separate gift or inheritance tax either. Gifts between individuals, family or not, generally come with no tax concern.
faq.a7kg: In Kyrgyzstan, property received by inheritance or gift from "close relatives" — spouse, parents, children, siblings, grandparents, grandchildren — is tax-exempt (except when received in the course of business activity). Gifts from non-relatives may be added to ordinary personal income and taxed.
faq.a7mm: Myanmar has no separate gift or inheritance tax — gifts received without consideration aren't even counted as capital gains, so they're exempt in principle.
faq.a7bd: Under Bangladesh's Gift Tax Act 1990, Section 4, gifts between close family — spouse, parents, children, siblings — are exempt. Other gifts get a basic exemption of up to Tk 20,000 per year, with progressive rates above that.
faq.a7pk: Under Pakistan's Income Tax Ordinance Section 39, gifts received from a "relative" (as defined in Section 85(5)) — grandparents, parents, spouse, siblings, children — are exempt. But the gift must come through a banking channel (crossed cheque, bank transfer); handing over cash directly forfeits the exemption and it can be taxed as "income from other sources."
faq.a7kh: ⚠️ We couldn't find a clear gift-tax provision in Cambodian law covering family gifts between individuals — Cambodia's territorial tax system generally means no general rule taxing personal gifts has been confirmed. If you're planning to share a large sum, be sure to check your specific situation with a local tax advisor.
faq.a7mn: Mongolia has no separate gift or inheritance tax. One exception: gifts an employer gives to an employee or their family can be treated as taxable employment income — but that's a different situation from a purely personal family gift.
faq.a7la: ⚠️ Under Laos's new Income Tax Law (effective July 2026), gift/prize income is reportedly exempt up to 5 million kip with a flat 5% rate above that — though it's unclear whether family gifts are treated differently from gifts to non-relatives, so confirm the exact scope with a Lao tax advisor.

faq.aud.us.q1: I'm a US citizen/green card holder living abroad — should I still use the US basis?
faq.aud.us.a1: Yes. The US is one of the few countries with “citizenship-based taxation,” so citizens and green card holders must report worldwide income (including this jackpot) to the US no matter where they live. This is one of the rare cases where tax obligation is tied to citizenship/status rather than residence, so don't assume living abroad frees you from US tax. You may also be taxed by your country of residence, so check that country's tax treaty and foreign tax credit rules too.
faq.aud.us.q2: I haven't been in the US long — do I still owe US tax?
faq.aud.us.a2: Short-term visitors classified as nonresident aliens usually just have the 30% withholding, but if you exceed the “Substantial Presence Test,” you're treated as a US tax resident and taxed like a citizen on worldwide income at graduated rates (up to 37%). The test is met if (1) you were present at least 31 days this year, and (2) all days this year + 1/3 of last year's days + 1/6 of the year before's days add up to 183 or more — it's a weighted 3-year calculation, not simply “183 days.” Students (some F/J visas), diplomats, etc. have exceptions, so consult a professional.
faq.aud.vn.q1: I'm a Vietnamese citizen living in another country — should I use the Vietnam basis?
faq.aud.vn.a1: Vietnam taxes based on residence: if you haven't actually stayed 183+ days in a year (or rolling 12 months) and have no registered residence there, you're generally a non-resident with no Vietnamese domestic filing duty (the 30% already withheld in the US still stands). If you actually live in Vietnam, just use the “Vietnam” basis.
faq.aud.vn.q2: I just arrived in Vietnam — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.vn.a2: Staying 183+ days in a year (or rolling 12 months), or maintaining a residence that meets the legal criteria, makes you a tax resident, taxed on worldwide income (including this jackpot). Under 183 days makes you a non-resident, taxed only on Vietnam-source income at a flat 20%. Vietnamese residents' prize income is reportedly taxed at 10% on the portion over 10 million VND per prize — whether this applies identically to a foreign lottery win is worth confirming with a professional.
faq.aud.cn.q1: I'm a Chinese citizen living in another country — should I use the China basis?
faq.aud.cn.a1: China also taxes based on residence, but its law treats anyone who habitually resides in China due to household registration (hukou), family, or economic ties as having a “domicile,” and may still count them as a resident regardless of actual days abroad. So if you keep your hukou and family/economic ties in China, you may not be recognized as a non-resident even while living overseas — this is case-by-case, so consult a professional. If you have no hukou (or have fully emigrated) and stayed under 183 days, you're a non-resident and foreign income isn't taxed by China.
faq.aud.cn.q2: I just arrived in China — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.cn.a2: China's 2019 tax law reform introduced a “six-year rule”: a non-domiciled foreigner is only taxed on worldwide income starting the 7th consecutive year of staying 183+ days each year (the count resets if you leave for more than 30 consecutive days in any year). So if you've been there under 6 years, foreign income like this jackpot generally isn't taxed by China. The count started in 2019, and 7th-year cases are only now starting to appear.
faq.aud.in.q1: I'm an Indian citizen living in another country (NRI) — should I use the India basis?
faq.aud.in.a1: India taxes based on residence too: if you stayed under 182 days in India in a financial year (April–March), you're classified NRI, and foreign income (including this jackpot) generally isn't taxed by India — only India-source income is.
faq.aud.in.q2: I just arrived in India — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.in.a2: Staying 182+ days in a financial year makes you a resident, taxed on worldwide income. But if you recently moved to India or were abroad for a long time, you may qualify for an intermediate “RNOR” status (e.g., if you stayed under 730 days in India over the preceding 7 years, applicable for up to 3 years) — during this period, foreign income like this jackpot isn't taxed by India. Exact RNOR eligibility depends on your recent years of presence in India, so consult a professional.
faq.aud.id.q1: I'm an Indonesian citizen living in another country — should I use the Indonesia basis?
faq.aud.id.a1: Indonesia also taxes based on residence: if you stayed under 183 days within a 12-month period and have no residence or intent to reside in Indonesia, you're generally a non-resident, and foreign income (including this jackpot) isn't taxed there.
faq.aud.id.q2: I just arrived in Indonesia — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.id.a2: Staying over 183 days within a 12-month period (or intending to reside) makes you a resident, taxed 5–35% progressive on worldwide income. However, under the Omnibus Law (Law No.11/2020) implementing rules, recognized “foreign experts” in specific fields (e.g., STEM) with a proper work permit (RPTKA) and NPWP can be taxed only on Indonesia-source income for their first 4 years as a resident — this applies only to those meeting these specific criteria, not all work-visa holders, so check your visa/qualification.
faq.aud.ph.q1: I'm a Filipino citizen living abroad (OFW etc.) — should I use the Philippines basis?
faq.aud.ph.a1: The Philippines taxes resident citizens on worldwide income, but a “non-resident citizen” — working/staying abroad 183+ days a year with a valid OEC/POEA registration (including OFWs) — is taxed only on Philippine-source income as an exception. So foreign income like this jackpot isn't taxed by the Philippines.
faq.aud.ph.q2: I just arrived in the Philippines — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.ph.a2: Uniquely, even if you become a “resident alien” by staying 183+ days, the Philippines still doesn't tax your foreign income — under Philippine tax law (NIRC), only resident citizens are taxed on worldwide income; both resident and nonresident aliens are taxed only on Philippine-source income. So if you're not a Filipino citizen, no matter how long you've lived there, this jackpot isn't subject to Philippine domestic tax — this is an exception opposite to most other countries, easy to misunderstand.
faq.aud.th.q1: I'm a Thai citizen living in another country — should I use the Thailand basis?
faq.aud.th.a1: Thailand taxes based on residence too: staying under 180 days in a calendar year makes you a non-resident regardless of citizenship. However, since 2024 Thailand taxes residents on foreign income remitted into Thailand regardless of when it was earned (Revenue Department Orders Paw.161/2566, 162/2566) — so if you plan to remit this jackpot to a Thai account while living abroad, check both your residency status and the timing of remittance.
faq.aud.th.q2: I just arrived in Thailand — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.th.a2: Staying 180+ days in a calendar year makes you a Thai tax resident. Since the 2024 reform, residents' foreign income is reportedly taxed upon remittance to Thailand regardless of when it was earned (income earned before 2024 is exempt). ⚠️ However, I couldn't find clear official guidance on whether this rule applies to windfall-type income like lottery winnings the same way it applies to employment/investment income — some interpretations suggest keeping it in a foreign account avoids tax, but please consult a Thai tax professional for the exact treatment.
faq.aud.jp.q1: I'm a Japanese citizen living in another country — should I use the Japan basis?
faq.aud.jp.a1: Japan also taxes based on residence: if your base of living is abroad and you plan to live there a year or more, you're generally classified non-resident, and foreign income (including this jackpot) isn't taxed by Japan. If you actually live in Japan, just use the “Japan” basis.
faq.aud.jp.q2: I just arrived in Japan — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.jp.a2: A non-Japanese-national resident who has stayed in Japan 5 years or less (within the past 10 years) is classified “non-permanent resident” — foreign income is taxed only to the extent it's actually remitted to or paid in Japan (not the full amount). So keeping this jackpot in a foreign account without remitting it may avoid Japanese tax within the first 5 years. Past 5 years, you become a “permanent resident” taxpayer, taxed on worldwide income regardless of remittance. Consult a professional for exact remittance-scope determinations.
faq.aud.ru.q1: I'm a Russian citizen living in another country — should I use the Russia basis?
faq.aud.ru.a1: Russia taxes based on residence too: staying under 183 days in Russia within any rolling 12 months makes you a non-resident regardless of citizenship, taxed only on Russia-source income (flat 30%) — this jackpot from abroad isn't included.
faq.aud.ru.q2: I just arrived in Russia — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.ru.a2: Staying 183+ days within any rolling 12-month period (not necessarily the calendar year) makes you a resident, taxed 13% flat on worldwide income (non-residents under 183 days pay 30% on Russia-source income only). However, Russia suspended key provisions of the US–Russia tax treaty by presidential decree No.585 in 2023, so offsetting the 30% already withheld in the US via a Russian foreign tax credit may not be possible — factor in potential double taxation.
faq.aud.np.q1: I'm a Nepali citizen living in another country — should I use the Nepal basis?
faq.aud.np.a1: Nepal taxes based on residence too: if you stayed under 183 days in Nepal within a 12-month period and have no habitual place of abode there, you're generally a non-resident, and foreign income (including this jackpot) isn't taxed by Nepal.
faq.aud.np.q2: I just arrived in Nepal — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.np.a2: Staying 183+ days within a 12-month period (cumulative, need not be consecutive) or maintaining a habitual abode in Nepal makes you a resident, taxed on worldwide income. Under 183 days makes you a non-resident, taxed only on Nepal-source income at a flat 25%.
faq.aud.lk.q1: I'm a Sri Lankan citizen living in another country — should I use the Sri Lanka basis?
faq.aud.lk.a1: Sri Lanka taxes based on residence too: staying under 183 days in an assessment year (April–March) generally makes you a non-resident, and foreign income (including this jackpot) isn't taxed. However, if you were a resident for the 2 preceding consecutive years, you must be fully absent for 12 consecutive months (365 days) to be recognized as non-resident — brief visits alone may keep resident status.
faq.aud.lk.q2: I just arrived in Sri Lanka — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.lk.a2: Staying 183+ days in an assessment year (April–March) makes you a resident, taxed 6–36% progressive on worldwide income. Under 183 days makes you a non-resident, taxed only on Sri Lanka-source income.
faq.aud.uz.q1: I'm an Uzbek citizen living in another country — should I use the Uzbekistan basis?
faq.aud.uz.a1: Uzbekistan taxes based on residence too: staying under 183 days within a rolling 12 months generally makes you a non-resident, and foreign income (including this jackpot) isn't taxed there. However, even under 183 days, if you stayed in Uzbekistan longer than in any other single country, you may still be classified a resident as an exception.
faq.aud.uz.q2: I just arrived in Uzbekistan — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.uz.a2: Staying over 183 days within a rolling 12 months makes you a resident, taxed a flat 12% on worldwide income (non-residents pay 20% on Uzbekistan-source income only). A new special regime reportedly took effect from 2026, recognizing residency after just 30 days if you meet property-ownership conditions — this could make you a resident faster, so check the latest implementation.
faq.aud.kz.q1: I'm a Kazakh citizen living in another country — should I use the Kazakhstan basis?
faq.aud.kz.a1: Kazakhstan uniquely also looks at your “center of vital interests” (family, property, citizenship/permit) alongside days of presence — even under 183 days, you may be classified resident if these ties remain in Kazakhstan. If family and residence have fully moved abroad, you're more likely non-resident with foreign income untaxed, but this is case-by-case, so consult a professional.
faq.aud.kz.q2: I just arrived in Kazakhstan — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.kz.a2: Staying 183+ days within a rolling 12 months makes you a resident, taxed a flat 10% on worldwide income. Even under 183 days, having family/property (“center of vital interests”) in Kazakhstan may still classify you resident. Non-residents are generally taxed 20% on Kazakhstan-source income only.
faq.aud.kg.q1: I'm a Kyrgyz citizen living in another country — should I use the Kyrgyzstan basis?
faq.aud.kg.a1: Kyrgyzstan taxes based on residence too: staying under 183 days in a tax year (calendar year) generally makes you a non-resident, and foreign income (including this jackpot) isn't taxed there.
faq.aud.kg.q2: I just arrived in Kyrgyzstan — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.kg.a2: Staying 183+ days within a tax year (calendar year) makes you a resident, taxed a flat 10% on worldwide income (non-residents pay the same 10% rate but only on Kyrgyzstan-source income — the scope differs even though the rate matches).
faq.aud.mm.q1: I'm a Myanmar citizen living in another country — should I use the Myanmar basis?
faq.aud.mm.a1: Myanmar taxes based on residence too: staying under 183 days in a fiscal year (April–March) generally makes you a non-resident, and foreign income (including this jackpot) isn't taxed there.
faq.aud.mm.q2: I just arrived in Myanmar — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.mm.a2: Staying 183+ days in a fiscal year (April–March) makes you a resident foreigner, taxed on worldwide income at the same progressive rates as citizens. Under 183 days makes you a non-resident foreigner, taxed only on Myanmar-source income at a flat 10%.
faq.aud.bd.q1: I'm a Bangladeshi citizen living in another country — should I use the Bangladesh basis?
faq.aud.bd.a1: Bangladesh taxes based on residence too: staying under 182 days in an income year (and under 365 cumulative days over the preceding 4 years) generally makes you a non-resident, and foreign income (including this jackpot) isn't taxed there.
faq.aud.bd.q2: I just arrived in Bangladesh — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.bd.a2: Staying 182+ days in an income year (or 90+ days plus 365+ cumulative days over the preceding 4 years) makes you a resident, taxed on worldwide income. Below that makes you a non-resident, taxed only on Bangladesh-source income at a flat 30%.
faq.aud.pk.q1: I'm a Pakistani citizen living in another country — should I use the Pakistan basis?
faq.aud.pk.a1: Pakistan taxes based on residence too: staying under 183 days in a tax year (July–June), and not meeting the 120-day + 365-cumulative-day-over-4-years alternative test, generally makes you a non-resident, and foreign income (including this jackpot) isn't taxed there.
faq.aud.pk.q2: I just arrived in Pakistan — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.pk.a2: Staying 183+ days in a tax year (July–June), or 120+ days with 365+ cumulative days over the preceding 4 tax years, makes you a resident, taxed 0–35% progressive on worldwide income. Below that makes you a non-resident, taxed only on Pakistan-source income.
faq.aud.kh.q1: I'm a Cambodian citizen living in another country — should I use the Cambodia basis?
faq.aud.kh.a1: Cambodia also determines residency by days present (182 days in a tax year), but Cambodia has no comprehensive personal income tax system — it mainly taxes salary income (Tax on Salary). I couldn't find a clear statutory provision on how non-employment windfall income like lottery winnings is taxed for individuals — rather than assuming “not taxed,” please confirm with a Cambodian tax professional if this applies to you.
faq.aud.kh.q2: I just arrived in Cambodia — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.kh.a2: Staying over 182 days in a tax year (cumulative, need not be consecutive) reportedly makes you a resident, taxed progressively on worldwide salary income. However, since Cambodia's system centers on salary income, whether this applies to non-employment income like lottery winnings is unclear — needs confirmation.
faq.aud.mn.q1: I'm a Mongolian citizen living in another country — should I use the Mongolia basis?
faq.aud.mn.a1: Mongolia taxes based on residence too: staying under 183 days in a tax year with no residence in Mongolia generally makes you a non-resident, and foreign income (including this jackpot) isn't taxed there.
faq.aud.mn.q2: I just arrived in Mongolia — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.mn.a2: Staying 183+ days in a tax year, or owning a residence in Mongolia, makes you a resident, taxed on worldwide income (including this jackpot). Below that makes you a non-resident, taxed only on Mongolia-source income.
faq.aud.la.q1: I'm a Lao citizen living in another country — should I use the Laos basis?
faq.aud.la.a1: Laos taxes based on residence too: staying under 183 days in a calendar year generally makes you a non-resident, and foreign income (including this jackpot) isn't taxed there.
faq.aud.la.q2: I just arrived in Laos — do I already owe tax there?
faq.aud.la.a2: Staying over 183 days in a calendar year makes you a resident, taxed progressively (0–25%) on worldwide income. Below that makes you a non-resident, taxed only on Laos-source income.
faq.usMoneyQ: Aside from the lottery, might I have unclaimed money that's already mine in the US?
faq.usMoneyA: You might. Every US state runs its own unclaimed property program, so old bank accounts, wages, or insurance payouts often end up held by the state government. IRS tax refunds can also go unclaimed. Check the list below.
faq.usCheck1: Filed a US tax return in the last few years but never received a refund you were owed
faq.usCheck2: May have unclaimed wages, insurance payouts, or dividends from a state you used to live or work in
faq.usCheck3: Haven't checked an old US bank account, safe deposit box, or dividend in years
faq.usChecklistFooter: We can’t do the lookup for you — but we’ve linked you straight to the real official channels. Different sites need different verification (some just need your name, others need your SSN). Takes about 10 minutes to check.
faq.inMoneyQ: Aside from the lottery, might I have unclaimed money that's already mine in India?
faq.inMoneyA: You might. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) runs the UDGAM portal, which lets you search unclaimed deposits across multiple banks at once, and the IEPF under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs holds dividends and shares unclaimed for 7+ years. Check the list below.
faq.inCheck1: Have accounts at multiple banks, and one of them may not have had any activity for over 10 years
faq.inCheck2: Used to own shares but haven't checked the dividends or the shares themselves in a long time
faq.inChecklistFooter: We can’t do the lookup for you — but we’ve linked you straight to the real official channels. UDGAM needs your registered mobile number and an OTP; IEPF works best if you still have the folio number from an old share certificate. Takes about 10 minutes to check.
faq.bdMoneyQ: Aside from the lottery, might I have unclaimed money that's already mine in Bangladesh?
faq.bdMoneyA: You might. Bangladesh Bank publishes bank-by-bank lists of accounts with no transactions for 10+ years — we can't do the lookup for you, but you can check the lists yourself below.
faq.usCheck4: Had a retirement plan (401(k), pension) through an old US employer whose company closed or whose plan was terminated
faq.bdSearchTip: 💡 Tip: Instead of a search box, this site lists accounts as PDF files by bank. Open the PDF for the bank you used, then press Ctrl+F (or your browser's "Find on page" on mobile) and search for your name.
faq.q22: What does the bank ask for when I receive my winnings in a Korean account? 💱
faq.a22:
Receiving money from abroad into a Korean account is generally unrestricted — Korea's Foreign Exchange Transactions Act mainly regulates money going out of the country, so there's no advance reporting duty on the receiving end.

That said, if a large sum suddenly arrives, your bank may ask for source-of-funds documents (proof of the win, your US withholding statement, etc.) for anti-money-laundering purposes — it's worth having these ready. Transactions over US$10,000 are automatically reported to the National Tax Service and other authorities through the bank, so don't assume skipping a tax filing will go unnoticed — as explained above, this income is subject to comprehensive income tax reporting anyway.

For reference, under the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act, “resident” status is based on length of stay, not nationality — a foreign national who has stayed in Korea 6 months or more is generally treated as a resident, which covers most foreign residents here.

If you plan to send the money onward to family in another country, that's the opposite direction (Korea → abroad) and different rules apply — transfers over US$5,000 may require supporting documents, so it's best to check with your bank's foreign exchange desk before sending a large amount.

※ This is general practical guidance, not tax or legal advice — confirm the exact requirements and documents with your bank or the Bank of Korea's foreign exchange help line (02-759-5300).
home.splitNote: ※ Tax is recalculated on the per-winner share, not the total — in countries with progressive tax rates, this can work out better than taxing the full amount. If you really do win jointly, it's safer to formally agree on each person's share in advance.
